moon-jellyfish.name: Moon Jellyfish
moon-jellyfish.shortDescription: The most recognized jellyfish species worldwide, known for its translucent bell and gentle pulsating movement.
moon-jellyfish.description:
The Moon Jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) is one of the most widely recognized and abundant jellyfish species in the world's oceans. Its translucent, saucer-shaped bell can grow up to 40 cm in diameter, and features four distinctive horseshoe-shaped gonads visible through the bell.

Moon jellyfish are found in every ocean, thriving in coastal waters with temperatures between 6-31°C. They feed primarily on plankton, small fish, and other tiny organisms, captured by their short, delicate tentacles that line the bell margin.

Their gentle pulsating movement and ethereal glow under light make them a favorite in aquariums worldwide. Moon jellyfish have a relatively mild sting that is harmless to most humans, making them one of the most popular species for home jellyfish keeping.
moon-jellyfish.habitat: Coastal waters worldwide, temperate and tropical oceans

japanese-sea-nettle.name: Japanese Sea Nettle
japanese-sea-nettle.shortDescription: A striking species with golden-brown bell and flowing tentacles, prized for its dramatic trailing oral arms.
japanese-sea-nettle.description:
The Japanese Sea Nettle (Chrysaora pacifica) is one of the most visually spectacular jellyfish species found in the waters of the northwest Pacific, primarily around Japan. Distinguished by its golden to reddish-brown bell that can reach up to 30 cm in diameter, it trails long, flowing oral arms and marginal tentacles that can extend several meters.

This species inhabits bays, estuaries, and coastal waters around Japan and the broader northwest Pacific, often appearing in aggregations near the coast during summer and fall months. Japanese Sea Nettles play an important ecological role, serving as both predator of zooplankton and prey for larger marine animals like sea turtles and ocean sunfish.

Their dramatic appearance — a warm amber bell contrasted against deep blue water, with ribbon-like oral arms streaming behind — makes them one of the most photographed jellyfish species. In aquariums, they are prized for their mesmerizing beauty and graceful swimming motion. They possess a moderate sting that can cause discomfort in humans but is rarely dangerous.
japanese-sea-nettle.habitat: Northwest Pacific Ocean, primarily around Japan
japanese-sea-nettle.size: Bell diameter: up to 30 cm, tentacles up to 3 m
japanese-sea-nettle.stingLevel: Moderate - can cause pain and welts

spotted-jellyfish.name: Spotted Jellyfish
spotted-jellyfish.shortDescription: A charming tropical species with a rounded bell decorated in white spotted patterns and eight frilly oral arms.
spotted-jellyfish.description:
The Spotted Jellyfish (Mastigias papua), also known as the Lagoon Jellyfish or Papua Jellyfish, is a stunningly beautiful species native to the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific. Its rounded, dome-shaped bell is decorated with distinctive white or pale spotted patterns on a translucent brown or blue-green background, growing up to 12 cm in diameter.

Unlike many jellyfish, Mastigias papua harbors symbiotic zooxanthellae algae within its tissues — the same type of photosynthetic organisms found in corals. This relationship provides the jellyfish with a significant portion of its nutrition through photosynthesis, supplementing its diet of small plankton. In some isolated marine lakes, entire populations have evolved to follow the sun across the water to maximize photosynthesis for their algal symbionts.

The Spotted Jellyfish has eight elaborate, frilly oral arms rather than long trailing tentacles, giving it a distinctive rounded silhouette. Its sting is extremely mild and virtually imperceptible to humans, making it one of the most popular and safe species for aquarium display.
spotted-jellyfish.habitat: Indo-Pacific tropical waters, marine lakes, lagoons
spotted-jellyfish.diet: Zooplankton, supplemented by symbiotic algae photosynthesis
spotted-jellyfish.stingLevel: Very mild - virtually imperceptible to humans

flame-jellyfish.name: Flame Jellyfish
flame-jellyfish.shortDescription: A large, edible jellyfish with a thick dome-shaped bell and bushy oral arms, widely cultivated in East Asia.
flame-jellyfish.description:
The Flame Jellyfish (Rhopilema esculentum) is one of the most commercially important jellyfish species in the world, widely harvested and cultivated across East Asia for culinary use. Its thick, robust bell can grow up to 50 cm in diameter, with a milky white to pale brown coloration and dense, cauliflower-like oral arms.

Native to the coastal waters of the western Pacific, particularly the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and waters around Japan and Korea, this species thrives in warm, shallow coastal environments. Rhopilema esculentum has been a staple of Chinese cuisine for centuries and is considered a delicacy when prepared as a cold dish with sesame oil and vinegar.

Beyond its culinary value, the Flame Jellyfish is increasingly popular in aquarium displays due to its impressive size and dramatic appearance. Its thick bell pulses with powerful, deliberate contractions, creating a mesmerizing visual effect. The species has a mild sting that is harmless to humans.
flame-jellyfish.habitat: Western Pacific, Yellow Sea, East China Sea

egg-yolk-jellyfish.name: Egg Yolk Jellyfish
egg-yolk-jellyfish.shortDescription: A large, distinctive jellyfish resembling a fried egg, with a yellow central mass surrounded by a translucent bell.
egg-yolk-jellyfish.description:
The Egg Yolk Jellyfish (Phacellophora camtschatica) is one of the most recognizable jellyfish in the ocean, named for its striking resemblance to a fried egg. Its large, flat bell can reach up to 60 cm in diameter, featuring a distinctive yellow-orange central mass of gonads surrounded by a translucent, whitish bell margin.

Found in temperate waters across the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, this species drifts slowly through the water column, often appearing nearly motionless. Unlike more active hunters, the Egg Yolk Jellyfish is a passive predator, using its long, delicate tentacles — which can trail up to 6 meters — to ensnare small jellyfish, zooplankton, and other gelatinous organisms that drift into contact.

In aquariums, the Egg Yolk Jellyfish is a showstopper due to its unusual form and enormous size. Its gentle, slow pulsing and dramatic trailing tentacles create an otherworldly display. The sting is very mild, posing minimal risk to humans.
egg-yolk-jellyfish.size: Bell diameter: up to 60 cm, tentacles up to 6 m
egg-yolk-jellyfish.stingLevel: Very mild - minimal risk to humans

pacific-sea-nettle.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
pacific-sea-nettle.shortDescription: A spectacular species with a golden-red bell and long, flowing tentacles, iconic along the Pacific coast.
pacific-sea-nettle.description:
The Pacific Sea Nettle (Chrysaora fuscescens) is one of the most visually stunning jellyfish species found along the Pacific coast of North America. Its golden to reddish-brown bell can reach up to 30 cm in diameter, with striking reddish-maroon oral arms and long, trailing marginal tentacles that can extend several meters.

This species inhabits the eastern Pacific Ocean from Alaska to Baja California, often appearing in large blooms near the coast during summer and fall months. Pacific Sea Nettles play an important ecological role as both predator of zooplankton and prey for larger marine animals like sea turtles and ocean sunfish.

Their dramatic appearance — a warm amber bell with deep crimson oral arms contrasted against blue water — makes them one of the most photographed and admired jellyfish species worldwide. In aquariums, they are a perennial favorite. They possess a moderate sting that can cause pain and welts in humans but is rarely dangerous.
pacific-sea-nettle.habitat: Eastern Pacific Ocean, from Alaska to Baja California
pacific-sea-nettle.size: Bell diameter: up to 30 cm, tentacles up to 4.5 m
pacific-sea-nettle.stingLevel: Moderate - can cause pain and welts
